anomaly_def.Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers fall behind because they cannot ingest, persist, or apply WAL/redo records as fast as the primary generates them.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical volumes servicing data, log, and temp files reach or exceed their read-write throughput limits, sharply increasing I/O latency and queue depth.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database-related processes saturate host CPU cycles, driving run-queue pressure and elevating CPU wait events across the workload.

When all three root causes occur together, the database exhibits a compound failure surface: replicas show rapidly widening log-position gaps while both primary and replica servers report soaring I/O latency and near-full CPU utilization. Check-point and log-flush operations slow down, causing the primary to retain ever-growing segments, which in turn inflate storage usage and further stress disk throughput. Queries on both primary and replicas experience multi-facet waits—first on CPU scheduling, then on disk service, and finally on replication consistency—causing erratic response-time spikes, missed SLAs, and compromised failover readiness. Monitoring views may alternate between I/O, CPU, and replication wait states, masking which layer is dominant at any given moment and making single-symptom diagnosis unreliable.

Causal chain: Saturated storage extends write-flush times; longer fsync or write-batch completion forces the primary to hold WAL segments open, inflating the volume of data that replicas must eventually consume. Because storage limits also slow replica redo reads, apply lag grows even faster. Simultaneously, high CPU usage—whether driven by heavy user workload, redo apply threads, or I/O polling—steals cycles from both the log-writer and replication receiver, elongating commit paths and apply loops. The CPU bottleneck aggravates storage saturation by limiting the dispatch rate of async I/O, while prolonged I/O waits keep worker threads runnable and spinning, compounding CPU load. The intertwined feedback loops of CPU starvation, disk congestion, and replication backlog amplify each other, producing a severe, self-reinforcing degradation that impacts both primary and replica nodes across transactional and analytical activity.

entry.official_definition: Terminates any session that has been idle within an open transaction for longer than the specified amount of time.
entry.trigger_condition: A session is idle, waiting for a client query, while an open transaction remains active longer than the configured threshold.
entry.workload_impact: The session is terminated; this prevents long idle transactions from holding locks or preventing vacuum cleanup.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
